questions.stem: During a rural health camp screening in India, a 6-year-old boy is evaluated for developmental delay and unusual skeletal features. His parents report that he has a history of frequent eye and vision issues. A genetic enzymatic defect is suspected. Which condition is associated with a defect in the enzyme cystathionine synthase?
questions.solutionHtml:
="font-family:"Calibri",sans-serif">Treatment: Diet low in methionine and rich in cysteine. In few cases, pyridoxal phosphate given in large quantities (500 mg).

 

Explanation:

 

Option A. Hartnup’s disease: Due to defective absorption of aromatic amino acids from intestine as well as reabsorption from renal tubules due to mutation of SLC6A19 gene encodes the transporter protein (B0AT1) seen in Intestine and renal tubules →excretion of amino acids in urine. Due to deficiency of Tryptophan, Niacin is not produced and so, the presentation is similar to Pellagra.

 

Option B. Cystinuria: Due to defect/deficiency of transporter system →patients cannot reabsorb cysteine into their bloodstream  → accumulation of cystine in urine forms crystals and stones → leads to recurrent nephrolithiasis and obstruction of urine flow →c/f- severe, sudden flank pain, blood and WBC in urine, fever, and finally renal failure.

 

Option D. Cystathioninuria: Due to cystathionine deficiency, patient presents with mental retardation, anemia, thrombocytopenia and endocrinopathies. Acquired Cystathioninuria might be due to pyridoxine deficiency, liver diseases and after thyroxine administration.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Cystathionine synthase is an enzyme critical in the metabolism of methionine, converting homocysteine to cystathionine. A deficiency in this enzyme leads to homocystinuria, a disorder characterized by elevated levels of homocysteine, which can result in developmental delay, skeletal abnormalities, and ocular issues.

questions.stem: Which group among the following is responsible for buffering activity of proteins at physiological pH?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Imidazole group

 

Option D:

 

The imidazole group, which is part of the histidine amino acid side chain, has significant buffering capacity at physiological pH (around 7.4). This is because the pKa of the imidazole group is close to the physiological pH, allowing it to effectively donate or accept protons, thereby contributing to buffering.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A: Sulfhydryl group - Present in cysteine, important for forming disulfide bonds, but not primarily known for buffering.

 

Option B: Indole group - Found in tryptophan, contributes to the protein's structural and functional aspects but lacks significant buffering capacity.

 

Option C: Phenyl group - Part of phenylalanine, contributes to hydrophobic interactions in proteins but does not have a buffering role.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Only amino acid whose pKa value (6.1) is nearby physiological pH (7.4) is Histidine (Imidazole group), due to which it has buffering activity at physiological pH.

 

 

Ref: Vasudevan 9/e: p 28.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the isoelectric pH (pI) of a molecule is INCORRECT?

options.label: A
options.text: The molecule carries no net charge

options.label: B
options.text: Solubility and buffering capacity will be maximum

options.label: C
options.text: The buffering capacity of plasma proteins are mainly due to Histidine residue.

options.label: D
options.text: There is no mobility in an electric field

questions.answerText: Solubility and buffering capacity will be maximum
questions.solutionHtml:
t">Option A: The molecule carries no net charge - This is correct. At the isoelectric point, the number of positive charges equals the number of negative charges, resulting in no net charge.

 

Option C: The buffering capacity of plasma proteins is mainly due to Histidine residue - This statement is generally correct as histidine residues in proteins, such as those in plasma proteins, play a significant role in buffering due to the pKa of the histidine side chain being close to physiological pH.

 

Option D: There is no mobility in an electric field - This is correct. Since the molecule has no net charge at its isoelectric point, it will not move towards either electrode in an electric field.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The pH at which the molecule carries no net charge is called an isoelectric point or isoelectric pH (pI).
  • At an isoelectric point, the amino acid will carry no net charge, all the groups are ionized but the charges will cancel each other. Hence, at isoelectric point, there is no mobility in an electrical field.
  • Solubility and buffering capacity will be minimum at isoelectric pH.
  • The buffering capacity of plasma proteins and hemoglobin is mainly due to histidine residue.

 

Ref: Harper 30/e: p 20.

The presence of characteristic hexagonal crystals in the urine along with RBCs, pus cells, and WBC casts suggests a stone-forming condition. questions.stem: In a study group session focusing on stereochemistry in biological molecules, a debate arises regarding the chiral properties of amino acids. One of the points of discussion is whether tyrosine, known for its aromatic ring and role in protein structure, possesses double chirality. Is the statement "Amino acid with double chiral centers is Tyrosine" true or false?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) False

 

Option B:

 

Tyrosine is an amino acid that contains only one chiral center, which is the alpha carbon atom common to all standard amino acids (except glycine, which is achiral). The presence of a single chiral center does not make tyrosine a compound with double chirality. Amino acids like threonine and isoleucine have two chiral centers, making them capable of having more stereoisomers.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The α-carbon of amino acids has four different groups attached to it and so is a chiral or asymmetric carbon
  • All amino acids have one chiral carbon, except-

 

  1. Amino acid with no chiral carbon → Glycine
  2. Amino acid with two chiral centers → Threonine & isoleucine

 

Ref: Vasudevan 9/e: p 29.

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B. TMS is less sensitive in screening for PKU than the bacterial inhibition tests

 

This statement is incorrect. Tandem Mass Spectrometry (TMS) is actually more sensitive and specific than bacterial inhibition tests (such as the Guthrie test) for detecting phenylketonuria (PKU).

 

Tandem Mass Spectrometry (TMS) has revolutionized newborn screening by providing higher sensitivity and specificity for detecting PKU and other metabolic disorders compared to older methods. TMS can directly measure phenylalanine levels and the phenylalanine-to-tyrosine ratio, which is more accurate for PKU detection than bacterial inhibition assays. The older bacterial inhibition tests had higher rates of false positives and were less precise in quantifying metabolite levels.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. TMS is the best screening test to detect the metabolic disorders - CORRECT TMS is indeed considered the gold standard for newborn metabolic screening. It can simultaneously detect multiple metabolic disorders by analyzing amino acids, acylcarnitines, and other metabolites from a single blood spot with high sensitivity and specificity.

 

Option C. Blood obtained by heel-prick or cord blood is applied to a filter-paper - CORRECT Newborn screening typically involves collecting a few drops of blood from the infant's heel (heel-prick) or from the umbilical cord at birth. This blood is then applied to special filter paper (Guthrie cards) and allowed to dry before being sent to the laboratory for analysis.

 

Option D. Has capacity to screen multiple disorders with a single blood spot - CORRECT This is one of the major advantages of TMS. Unlike earlier screening methods that required separate tests for each disorder, TMS can simultaneously screen for dozens of metabolic disorders (including amino acid disorders, fatty acid oxidation disorders, and organic acidemias) using just a single blood spot.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The sensitivity of tandem MS-MS testing in screening for PKU is greater than the sensitivity of any bacterial inhibition or biochemical method for measuring blood phenylalanine levels. The power of new-born screening by tandem MS-MS is enormously enhanced by the ability to analyze several metabolites simultaneously in the same blood specimen.

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Presence of a white patch of hair is due to a deficiency in tryptophan

 

Option C:

 

This case describes a newborn with classic physical features of phenylketonuria (PKU) - blue eyes, blond hair, and fair skin - who has tested positive on the Guthrie test, a screening test for elevated phenylalanine levels.

 

Statement C is incorrect because the hypopigmentation (lighter hair and skin) seen in PKU is not related to tryptophan deficiency. Rather, it results from Reduced tyrosine availability (since phenylalanine cannot be converted to tyrosine)

Tryptophan is an essential amino acid involved in serotonin synthesis, but it does not play a direct role in the pigmentation pathways affected in PKU.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Due to deficiency of enzyme Phenylalanine Hydroxylase: This statement is true. PKU is caused by mutations in the gene encoding phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH), which normally converts phenylalanine to tyrosine. Without functional PAH, phenylalanine accumulates to toxic levels in the body.

 

Option B. Mental retardation is a potential complication: This statement is true. Untreated PKU can lead to significant intellectual disability due to the neurotoxic effects of elevated phenylalanine and its metabolites. Early diagnosis and dietary management can prevent this outcome.

 

Option D. Phenylacetate is found in the urine: This statement is true. In PKU, the excess phenylalanine is metabolized through alternative pathways, producing phenylketones including phenylpyruvate, phenyllactate, and phenylacetate, which are excreted in the urine. The presence of these compounds gives PKU its name and produces the characteristic "musty" or "mousy" odor.

 

Educational Objective: 

 

Phenylketonuria results from phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency, causing elevated phenylalanine levels and reduced tyrosine. The hypopigmentation seen in PKU patients is due to impaired melanin synthesis from reduced tyrosine availability—not from tryptophan deficiency. Early detection through newborn screening and prompt dietary management are essential to prevent the neurological sequelae of this inborn error of metabolism.

questions.stem: Following routine newborn screening, a child is found to have high levels of phenylpyruvate and phenylacetate, indicative of phenylketonuria (PKU). Despite a phenylalanine-restricted diet, the child shows developmental delays. Which supplement might improve the child's condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
. A. Tyrosine

 

Explanation: 

 

Phenylketonuria (PKU) results from a deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH), the enzyme that converts phenylalanine to tyrosine. This deficiency leads to:

  1. Accumulation of phenylalanine and its metabolites (phenylpyruvate, phenylacetate, phenyllactate)
  2. Reduced tyrosine production, making tyrosine an essential amino acid in PKU patients

 

In PKU treatment, dietary phenylalanine restriction is the primary approach to prevent neurotoxicity from excess phenylalanine. However, this restriction alone can lead to tyrosine deficiency, as tyrosine can no longer be synthesized from phenylalanine.

 

Tyrosine is critical for:

  • Production of neurotransmitters (dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine)
  • Synthesis of thyroid hormones
  • Melanin production

 

Tyrosine supplementation is therefore beneficial in PKU management as it:

  • Addresses the conditionally essential status of tyrosine
  • Supports neurotransmitter synthesis, potentially improving neurological function
  • May reduce the risk of developmental delays associated with tyrosine deficiency

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. 5-hydroxytryptophan: This is a precursor to serotonin in the tryptophan metabolism pathway. While serotonin levels might be indirectly affected in PKU due to competition between elevated phenylalanine and tryptophan for transport across the blood-brain barrier, supplementing with 5-hydroxytryptophan does not address the primary biochemical defect or the tyrosine deficiency in PKU.

 

Option C. Melanin: This is an end product of tyrosine metabolism and not a supplement that would provide therapeutic benefit in PKU. The hypopigmentation sometimes seen in PKU patients is due to reduced tyrosine availability for melanin synthesis, but direct melanin supplementation would not address the metabolic or neurological issues.

 

Option D. Phenylalanine: Supplementing with phenylalanine would be contraindicated in PKU as it would exacerbate the condition. PKU patients already have elevated phenylalanine levels due to impaired metabolism, and additional phenylalanine would increase toxic metabolite production and neurological damage.

 

Educational Objective: 

 

In phenylketonuria, phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency creates a metabolic block in converting phenylalanine to tyrosine. While dietary phenylalanine restriction is the mainstay of treatment, supplementation with tyrosine is important because it becomes an essential amino acid in this condition. Tyrosine supplementation supports neurotransmitter synthesis, and potentially improves developmental outcomes by addressing the "downstream" deficiency caused by the enzymatic block.

 

Ref: DM Vasudevan 9/e: p 236.

Explanation:

 

Option A. Acidosis due to elevated phenyllactate: While acidosis can have deleterious effects on the body and can be a feature of organic acidemias, it is not the primary reason for developmental delays in conditions like phenylketonuria. Acidosis is more of an acute metabolic disturbance rather than a direct cause of chronic developmental issues.

 

Option B. Lack of tyrosine, now an essential amino acid: Tyrosine is a precursor for several neurotransmitters, and while its deficiency due to a block in conversion from phenylalanine can impact brain function, the developmental delay is more directly linked to the broader competition of phenylalanine with other LNAAs, rather than tyrosine deficiency alone.

 

Option C. Inhibition of hydroxylating enzymes due to accumulation of phenylalanine: Phenylalanine can indeed inhibit certain enzymes, including hydroxylating enzymes, due to its elevated levels. This can have various metabolic effects, but the specific link to developmental delay is less direct compared to the competition of phenylalanine with other LNAAs for transport into the brain.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Elevated levels of phenylalanine are known to interfere with the transport of other large, neutral amino acids (LNAAs) across the blood-brain barrier due to competitive inhibition. These LNAAs include tyrosine, tryptophan, and others that are precursors for key neurotransmitters essential for brain development and function. A deficiency in these neurotransmitters can result in developmental delays.

The clinical features of tyrosinemia type I, includes failure to thrive, poor appetite, hepatomegaly, jaundice, vomiting, diarrhea, and a distinct odor resembling cabbage due to the accumulation of tyrosine metabolites.

questions.stemHtml: A newborn present with milky white skin, white hair, and red-appearing eyes. Which enzyme defect is most commonly associated with this disorder?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Tyrosinase

 

Option C:

 

The clinical presentation described (milky white skin, white hair, and red-appearing eyes) is characteristic of oculocutaneous albinism (OCA). This condition results from a deficiency of tyrosinase, a copper-containing enzyme that catalyzes the steps in melanin biosynthesis:

 

Tyrosinase is critical for melanin production in melanocytes. Without functional tyrosinase, melanin synthesis is impaired or absent, resulting in hypopigmentation of the skin, hair, and eyes.

 

The red-appearing eyes are due to the absence of melanin in the iris, allowing the blood vessels of the retina to be visible.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Phenylalanine hydroxylase: Deficiency of this enzyme leads to phenylketonuria, which is characterized by an inability to metabolize phenylalanine, leading to intellectual disability and other problems, not albinism.

 

Option B. NADPH oxidase: Defects in this enzyme are associated with chronic granulomatous disease, which affects the immune system, not pigmentation.

 

Option D. Homogentisic acid oxidase: A defect in this enzyme results in alkaptonuria, which leads to the buildup of homogentisic acid causing dark urine and possibly ochronosis, but not albinism.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Albinism is most often caused by a defect in the enzyme tyrosinase, leading to a lack of melanin production and the associated clinical presentation of white skin, white hair, and red-appearing eyes.

 

Ref: DM Vasudevan 9/e: p 234,238.

Option B Homogentisate Oxidase →Alkaptonuria (AR inheritance) →results in excretion of homogentisic acid in urine. C/F- blackening of urine on standing, Ochronosis and Black pigments over joint cavities to produce arthritis.

Educational Objective:

 

Melanin synthesis requires the enzyme tyrosinase, which catalyzes the oxidation of tyrosine to DOPA and DOPAquinone, key steps in the production of melanin. A deficiency or functional impairment in tyrosinase can lead to conditions like vitiligo or albinism, characterized by the loss of pigmentation in the skin.

Kynurenine is formed from the catabolism of tryptophan via the kynurenine pathway. span style="font-size:12.0pt">Explanation:

Option B. Dopamine: Elevated levels of dopamine in urine could indicate a neuroendocrine tumor, like a pheochromocytoma, but this patient's symptoms align more closely with carcinoid syndrome.

 

Option D. Cortisol: While cortisol can be measured in urine to test for Cushing's syndrome, the symptoms here are not typical of Cushing's syndrome, which usually includes features such as weight gain, fat distribution changes, and sometimes hypertension.

24-hour urinary excretion of 5-HIAA is a useful diagnostic test for carcinoid syndrome.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the outpatient department by his parents due to concerns about his behavioral problems. Upon examination, the physician notes several physical anomalies: brittle and coarse hair, red patches on the skin, disproportionately long and thin arms and legs, scoliosis, a displaced lens, and muscular hypotonia. Given these clinical findings, which metabolite is most likely to be elevated in this patient's blood work?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D. Homocysteine

 

Option D:

 

The clinical presentation described is classic for homocystinuria, an inborn error of metabolism typically caused by a deficiency of cystathionine β-synthase (CBS). This enzyme catalyzes the condensation of homocysteine and serine to form cystathionine in the pathway of methionine metabolism.

 

Key clinical features of homocystinuria presented in this case include:

  • Ocular manifestations: Ectopia lentis (displaced lens)
  • Skeletal abnormalities: Marfanoid habitus (disproportionately long limbs), scoliosis.
  • Neurodevelopmental issues: Behavioral problems, muscular hypotonia
  • Dermatological findings: Brittle and coarse hair, red patches on skin

 

In CBS deficiency, homocysteine cannot be converted to cystathionine, resulting in elevated homocysteine levels in the blood and urine. Elevated homocysteine leads to multisystem effects including vascular damage, connective tissue abnormalities, and neurological complications.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Methionine: While methionine levels are also typically elevated in homocystinuria (as it's the precursor to homocysteine in the metabolic pathway), homocysteine is the more direct and characteristic metabolite associated with the clinical manifestations. Methionine elevation is secondary to the metabolic block and not the primary cause of symptoms.

 

Option B. Phenylpyruvate: This metabolite is elevated in phenylketonuria (PKU), which presents with fair skin, eczema, and intellectual disability, but typically lacks the skeletal abnormalities, ectopia lentis, and Marfanoid habitus seen in this patient.

 

Option C. Fibrillin: This is a structural protein, not a metabolite measured in blood work. Mutations in the fibrillin-1 gene cause Marfan syndrome, which shares some features with homocystinuria (tall stature, ectopia lentis, skeletal abnormalities) but is a connective tissue disorder, not a metabolic condition with abnormal blood metabolites.

 

Educational Objective: 

 

Homocystinuria due to cystathionine β-synthase deficiency presents with a constellation of findings including ectopia lentis, Marfanoid habitus (tall, thin build with long extremities), skeletal abnormalities, and neurodevelopmental issues. The biochemical hallmark is elevated homocysteine, which can be detected in blood and urine testing. Early diagnosis and treatment with vitamin B6 (pyridoxine), betaine, methionine restriction, and cysteine supplementation may prevent or minimize complications.

Option D. Serine to glycine: While the conversion of serine to glycine is part of amino acid metabolism and can feed into various pathways, it does not directly yield an intermediate that is as pivotal for both oxidative phosphorylation and gluconeogenesis as oxaloacetate.

Oxaloacetate is a critical intermediate in both gluconeogenesis, where it serves as a starting point for the synthesis of glucose, and in the citric acid cycle (TCA cycle) for oxidative phosphorylation. questions.stem: A 7-year-old child with a diagnosed urea cycle disorder presents with recurrent episodes of hyperammonemia, especially after high-protein meals. Despite dietary protein restriction and ammonia scavenging medications, the child's ammonia levels remain intermittently elevated, leading to concerns about long-term neurological outcomes. Which combination of supplements could provide an alternative pathway for nitrogen excretion and help manage the child's condition more effectively?

nt-size:11pt">Explanation:

 

Option A. Arginine and glutamine: Glutamine is often elevated in UCDs as it binds with free ammonia; however, supplementation with glutamine is not typically used for treatment because the body is already producing excess.

 

Option B. Lysine and glutamine: Lysine is not specifically involved in the urea cycle, and, as mentioned, glutamine is typically already elevated in UCDs.

 

Option D. Lysine and benzoate: Lysine is not a supplement used in the management of UCDs, and while benzoate is used, it would not be paired with lysine for treatment.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Urea cycle disorders (UCDs) result in the body's inability to properly dispose of waste nitrogen from protein metabolism, leading to hyperammonemia. Arginine supplementation can be beneficial because it provides an essential amino acid that is often deficient in UCDs.

 

Benzoate combines with glycine to form hippurate, which provides an alternative pathway for nitrogen excretion. This combination can help reduce ammonia levels in the blood by providing substrates for other nitrogen disposal pathways.
